title: Which side of the plane should you sit on flying to Hurghada?
author: Brogan
intro: Flying into Hurghada, the right side of the plane usually gives the best view, with the Red Sea, its coral reefs and the resort coast passing below as you come in to land. Here's why, when it changes and which seats to pick.
seo_title: Flying to Hurghada: sit on the right (usually)
seo_description: Usually the right side (seat F) for the Red Sea coast as you land at Hurghada. Why the north wind decides it, when it flips, and where to sit flying home.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
- **Best side:** right, seat F
- **Why:** landings usually head north
- **When it flips:** on rare southerly winds
- **Flight time:** about 5 to 5½ hrs

This is guidance, not a guarantee. The wind decides which way planes land, and air traffic control decides the exact route in, so no seat is certain. On most days, though, the odds are on the right.

sections.heading: Why the right side usually wins
sections.text:
Hurghada's airport sits just inland from the Red Sea coast, on the southern edge of the town. Its two parallel runways run roughly north to south, and the wind along this coast blows from the north on most days of the year. Planes land into the wind, so they normally use runway 34, approaching from the south and heading north.

On that final approach, the coast is on your **right** and the desert is on your left. From an F seat you may see the turquoise shallows and reefs, the resorts strung along the shore south of the town, and the Giftun islands offshore. From the left side, you mostly see the desert and the Red Sea Mountains beyond it.

Tip: flights from the UK arrive from the north, and some routes come down over the sea past Hurghada before turning in to land. On those, the right side gets the coast twice, but depending on the route you're given, the left side may glimpse El Gouna's lagoons on the way down.

sections.heading: How the approach usually works
sections.text:
| Wind | Runway used | Best side for the coast |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Northerly (most days) | 34, landing heading north | right (seat F) |
| Southerly (uncommon) | 16, landing heading south | left (seat A) |
| Light or changing winds | either | right is still the better bet |

On the less common days when planes land heading south, the approach comes in over the desert north of the town, and you may see little but sand until the last few minutes. You won't know in advance, so book the right and take what comes.

sections.heading: Which seats to choose
sections.text:
Where you sit along the plane matters almost as much as the side:

- **In front of the wing** gives the clearest view, but those rows often cost more to choose.
- **Behind the wing** is usually the best value, with a clear view down as the plane descends.
- **Over the wing**, the wing and engine block most of the view below.
- **Check the seat map:** some window seats on popular jets don't line up with a window at all.

On a Boeing 737 or Airbus A321, which most UK airlines use for Hurghada, the right window seat is **F** and the left is **A**. On a five-hour flight, paying for a seat you like is worth more than on a short hop, so a window behind the wing on the right is a good choice.

sections.heading: On the way home
sections.text:
Most departures take off towards the north, into the wind, and then head north-west for the UK, crossing the Red Sea Mountains and the Nile valley.

Which side gets the best view depends on the turn, so it varies from flight to flight. On a clear day you may see the coast and El Gouna on the climb out, and later the green strip of the Nile cutting through the desert.

Watch out: on daytime flights home, the sun is often on the left side of the plane heading north-west, so a right-hand seat can be more comfortable if you'd rather read or sleep.

sections.heading: What you might see
sections.text:
On a clear day, coming in to land you might spot:

- **The coral reefs**, as pale turquoise patches in the deep blue water just off the shore.
- **The Giftun islands**, a popular boat trip for snorkelling, a short way offshore from the town.
- **The resort coast**, with hotels and marinas stretching south of the town towards Sahl Hasheesh and Makadi Bay.
- **The Red Sea Mountains**, bare and rocky, running inland behind the desert.

The flight from the UK takes around five to five and a half hours, so it's worth having something to read for the first part, before the view begins.

sections.heading: Planning a trip to Hurghada?
sections.text:
Our [Hurghada guide](/destinations/hurghada) covers when to go, how long to stay and what to see. If you're deciding where to go in the Red Sea, our [Hurghada or Sharm el-Sheikh in winter](/blog/hurghada-or-sharm-el-sheikh-in-winter) post compares the two.

Flying somewhere else? See which side to sit on flying to [Tenerife](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on-flying-to-tenerife), [Gran Canaria](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on-flying-to-gran-canaria) or [Málaga](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on-flying-to-malaga), or our general guide to [which side of the plane to sit on](/blog/which-side-of-the-plane-to-sit-on).

faqs.question: Which side of the plane is best for landing at Hurghada?
faqs.answer: Usually the right side, seat F on most short-haul jets. On most days planes land heading north, with the Red Sea coast on the right and the desert on the left.

faqs.question: Do planes ever land the other way at Hurghada?
faqs.answer: Yes, on the less common days with southerly winds. Then they land heading south, and the coast is on the left, though you see less of it on that approach.

faqs.question: How long is the flight to Hurghada from the UK?
faqs.answer: About five to five and a half hours direct, a little longer from Scotland and the north of England.

faqs.question: Can you see the coral reefs from the plane?
faqs.answer: On a clear day, yes. The reefs show up as pale turquoise patches along the shore and around the islands, best seen from a window seat in front of or behind the wing.
